line: Afternoon. Gary Pruitt, from the Elm Street Neighborhood Association. You're new on the block, I think?
choice2: Isn't that the group that fought the clinic signs?
choice3: Nice to meet you. I should get going.

line: We didn't fight the bilingual signs. We asked who was paying for them. People heard what they wanted to hear.
The county, in the end. Out of the same pot as the potholes. I said so at a meeting, and somebody wrote to the paper that I was against signs. I'm against potholes.
choice1: What else does the association do?

line: Welcome. We meet second Tuesdays at the Legion hall on Sixth. Mostly parking and trash pickup, if you're wondering. It's not exciting.
choice1: What's the problem with trash pickup?

line: They moved pickup to Mondays without telling anybody, so half the block put their cans out on Thursday for a month. I got it moved back. Took four phone calls and a letter.
choice2: Do many people come to the meetings?
choice3: I'll keep an eye on the cans.

line: Twelve, fifteen. Mostly the same people for twenty years. People who've owned on this street a long time. We'd take more, if they showed up.

Not many. Some of them have their own thing over at {homeCenter}, which is fine. They've got their meetings, we've got ours. $ I don't think there's anything wrong with that. People like to be with people who know what they mean.
choice1: Wouldn't it help to meet together?
choice3: I'm not sure that's true for me.

line: On some things, maybe. The trash, sure. I've been to a couple of the joint nights at the library. Everybody's polite, everybody eats, then everybody goes home to their own street. I'd rather be honest about it.
choice2: That's one way to see it.

line: Morning. You have a minute? We're collecting signatures on the Fifth Street lot.
The city wants to sell it to a developer for a 'cultural plaza.' Fountain, stage, food stalls. Right now it's forty parking spaces, and the church and the diner need every one.
choice2: I'd want to hear both sides first.

line: That's fair. Read it, it's one page. Look, a plaza's not a bad idea. I just don't know whose culture it's for. Nobody asked the people who've lived here forty years.

The association. The church. The people who park there. I'm sure {homeCenter} has its own opinion and they're welcome to it. But it's our lot. $ [neutral] My mother walked to that diner every Sunday for thirty years. I'd like to keep it so somebody else can.
Afternoon. My knee again. Third time this month. They've got one doctor on Tuesdays, and five people working the whole place.
Five. I counted. The nurse at the desk does the phones and the shots both. I'm not complaining about her. She's the best thing here.
_nods at the signs on the wall_ We asked for a second doctor on Tuesdays, two years running. What we got was signs. I know the signs didn't cost a doctor. It still feels like that's what we got.
choice2: I can see why it feels that way.

line: Every year. Next time I'll bring the petition here, to the waiting room. Half this room would sign it, whatever language they read it in. _pauses_ That's the funny part.
choice1: Maybe bring it in a few languages.

line: Gary is pressing tape down on the association flyer on the lamppost with his thumb. "Third one this week. The wind takes them, or somebody does."
choice1: 'Keep the Fifth Street lot as parking'?

line: _shrugs_ Kids. The plaza people. Me, on a bad day, if I'd lost the vote. I don't accuse anybody. I just carry more tape.
You're all right, you know that? You come to things and you don't make a fuss.
Some people move in and want the whole street to change for them. You don't. You keep your things, we keep ours, and everybody says good morning.
choice1: Do you think people should keep apart?
choice2: I'm not sure it's that simple.

line: Apart's a strong word. Look, I don't have anything against anybody. I just think folks are happiest with their own. I'm happiest at the Legion on a Friday. You're probably happiest at {homeCenter}.
choice1: I'm not sure that's true for me.

line: No? _considers it_ Well. Then you're the exception, and that's fine too. My daughter married a man from two states over, and I still don't follow half of what his family talks about at Thanksgiving.
We need people at the association meeting tomorrow evening who actually live here and show up. You do both. Will you come sit with us?
Sit, listen, vote on the lot. Twelve folding chairs and a coffee urn. It'd help to have somebody younger. Most of us remember when the diner was a pharmacy.
Afternoon. Did you see the president last night?
choice3: I'd rather not get into it.

line: He's not wrong that rules should mean something. My grandfather came through Ellis Island with his papers in order. That's all I'm saying.
Maybe not. I don't want anybody dragged out of a house on my street, either. The family across from me, I don't ask, they don't tell me, and they shovel my walk.
_pauses_ Both, I guess. Rules for the country, and on my street I mind my own business. I don't know how those two fit together. I'm not sure anybody on TV does either.
choice1: Maybe they don't have to fit.

line: Now it's interpreters at the polling places.
Fine. Who trains them, and who pays? Nobody wants to answer the second question. I've asked twice, in writing.
choice2: Probably the same people who pay for everything else.

line: That's what they tell me. Meanwhile our request for two streetlights on Elm has been 'under review' since March. I'm not against anybody voting. I'd just like the streetlights.
Some days. I've lived here sixty-one years, and lately I go to the clinic and the signs are for somebody else. I'm not proud of how that feels. It's how it feels.
Haven't seen you at our meetings. I figure you've got your own thing over at {homeCenter}.
No complaint. I hear they do a lunch on weekends you can smell from the sidewalk. Is it any good?
choice2: You could come and try it.

line: Maybe someday. And I mean it, that's fine. Every group should have its place. Ours is twelve chairs at the Legion, theirs is over there. $ [guarded] I'd only say, don't let anybody tell you that you have to do both. Nobody can keep up with two.
People notice you around. Ellen in 4C says you carried her groceries up last week.
choice1: She had a lot of groceries.

line: Not anyone. Her own son lives in Phoenix. That's what a neighbourhood is, to me. Who carries what up the stairs.
choice2: Tell her I'm on the third floor if she needs me.

line: Mm. Hello.
choice1: Hi, Gary. No hard feelings about before.

line: None taken. People say things. I've said a few at meetings myself.
Can't stop, I've got flyers to put up before it rains.
Morning. I'm returning a book Ruth Hale told me I'd like. I didn't.
choice3: Better luck with the next one.

line: A novel about two families on one street. Ruth runs the programs here. The potluck, the citizenship class, the health fair. Anything that happens on this side of town, Ruth's behind it, and people go along.
choice1: You don't sound sure about her.
choice2: Sounds like she's good at it.

line: She's good at it. She's a fine woman. $ I just think she wants everybody at one table, and some people would rather have their own. I would. Nobody asks the twelve of us at the Legion, because Ruth's already got a flyer out.
choice1: You could go to one of her nights.

line: Morning. Our association breakfast got folded into Frank DeLuca's. Now it's the 'Fifth Street merchants' breakfast,' and I'm a merchant, apparently.
Hardware store. Frank runs Fifth, and lately the association too, because people listen to him. Good man. Sponsors the Little League.

But he wants everybody to be one thing. 'Become American, it worked for my grandfather.' $ I don't need anybody to become anything. I'd just like them to come to their own meetings and let us have ours.
Afternoon. Ruth Hale wants the association to co-host the block-party potluck. On our street.
We voted. Eight to four, yes. People around here don't say no to Ruth. She brings the flyers already printed, with your name on them.
I voted no. Not against her. I just think a block party's for the block. $ [neutral] I'll still carry the folding tables. Somebody has to, and Ruth knows I will.
Afternoon. Frank DeLuca has the association writing a letter about the signs at the clinic.
English first on every sign, big, and the rest small underneath. Frank wrote it, I typed it. When Frank wants a letter, people sign it.

I did. I want the second doctor more than I care about the signs, and Frank says he'll bring that up too. $ I'm not sure Frank and I want the same thing. He wants everybody the same. I'd settle for everybody minding their own.
choice1: Thanks for being straight with me.
